text: 250 years ago,
just under a mile from here,
Thomas Jefferson wrote
one of the most consequential documents
in American history.
Now, the Declaration of Independence wasn't perfect,
just like the guy who wrote it,
and the country it created weren't perfect either.
But it set us on this path, right?
This beautiful, audacious, complicated path that's still evolving.
And the Declaration of Independence still gives me chills.
“We hold these truths to be self-evident,
that all are created equal,
that they are endowed with certain unalienable rights,
and that among these are life,
liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.”
It's good, right?
(Laughter)
Did you get chills?
(Laughter)
I mean, yeah, I changed it a little, OK, from --
(Laughter)
"All men are created equal"
to "all are created equal"
because it makes it better, right?
Thank you.
(Applause)
And that's the point I want to talk with you about today,
that to live up to its promise,
we have evolved democracy in the past
and it needs to evolve again,
not only so that we can feel our votes count,
but so we can count democracy's real benefits
in our lives,
including in our wallets.
So a couple of years ago,
a philanthropic foundation in the United States
asked me to do some research
to find out why authoritarianism was gaining ground around the globe.
So I interviewed
civic leaders in West Africa and scholars in Eastern Europe
and democracy leaders in Latin America.
And I asked them,
What's authoritarianism getting so right?
These leaders that are pushing people and places away from democracy,
what are these authoritarians doing that's so effective?
And pretty much everyone I talked to said I was asking the wrong question --
that authoritarianism wasn’t surging because of anything it was doing right,
but because of what democracy was getting wrong.
That stopped me in my tracks.
The way they put it,
authoritarianism was like an opportunistic disease
that could only take root when democracy was weak.
And in case you haven't been paying attention --
(Laughter)
Democracy is kind of on life support.
So according to Freedom House,
only about 20 percent of the world's population
lives in a country currently that can be considered free.
And dissatisfaction with democracy is rising worldwide.
In the US, for instance,
about three out of five Americans say they are currently dissatisfied
with how democracy is working.
Why?
The answer came from a conversation I had with Kwasi Prempeh.
So Kwasi runs the Ghana Center for Democratic Development.
Now Ghana only won independence from colonial rule in 1957,
so not that long ago,
but long enough that most people in Ghana today
don't remember a time before democracy.
But what they do know
is that they're struggling economically right now under democracy.
And so, as Kwasi put it, they very understandably ask,
"What has democracy done for me lately?"
His point
is that democracies that do not deliver broad-based opportunity
are vulnerable to autocratic capture.
And research backs this up.
So Susan Stokes is a political science professor at the University of Chicago.
She has looked at variables for why democracy erodes in some countries,
but not others.
Income inequality
is the overwhelming variable in democratic backsliding,
so much so that Stokes said short of unplugging their computers,
they couldn't make it go away.
Now I want to be really clear about something.
In the richest country in the world,
a country that boasts about being a land of opportunity for all,
ensuring meaningful economic opportunity for all
is the right thing to do.
It is the moral thing to do,
and that is enough of a reason to do it.
And it's practical.
Economic justice is how we save democracy.
(Applause)
So I'm feeling like this might be as much of a revelation to you
as it was to me,
or at least it was maybe more of a revelation to me
than it was to you,
because we were used to, we have, for our 250 years,
thought of democracy and economic opportunity
as distinct and separate.
I mean, obviously interrelated,
and for many of us equally important,
but separate.
They're not.
They're two sides of the same coin.
Because if democracy doesn't deliver
meaningful economic opportunity,
democracy starts to feel meaningless.
And that makes authoritarianism and other forms of government more attractive,
not in and of themselves,
but by default,
because democracy is defaulting on its promise.
So I said before that we've evolved democracy in the past,
and it needs to evolve again.
I want us to think about democracy in phases.
Democracy 1.0 is that initial idea
that the people
should have the power in a political system,
not kings,
not empires,
not corporations,
the people.
It was a radical idea for its time.
Honestly, it's still really radical.
But as we know, that was just the beginning.
Democracy 2.0
is the phase where we expand
who is included in democracy, who gets to participate,
who counts as the people.
In the United States,
that process has been long.
It has taken generations of struggle --
abolition, suffrage, civil rights --
to make democracy more inclusive,
to say that everyone gets an equal vote
because everyone matters equally.
The brilliant scholar Isabel Wilkerson argues that, in fact,
the US wasn't even really a democracy until 1965,
when the Voting Rights Act became law.
And ever since then there has been an aggressive movement
to roll back that progress.
While we should be making more progress on democracy 2.0,
far-right extremists,
aided and abetted by the Supreme Court,
have dismantled the Voting Rights Act
and are trying to take us backwards.
So realistically,
while it makes sense to question
whether we even have a democracy right now in the United States,
either way,
we still tend to focus more
on democracy as a process
and not enough on what democracy produces.
On democratic outcomes.
We think and argue and talk a lot
about who gets to be included in democracy,
but not enough about why.
Why do we have a democracy in the first place?
Answering that question --
defining the goal of democracy --
that's democracy 3.0.
Democracy 3.0 says
that if all of us were truly created equal,
and if all of us truly get
to participate equally,
then the outcomes of our democracy
should be more equitable, too, right?
More widely shared and benefiting everyone.
(Applause)
But --
(Laughter)
Did you hear it coming?
(Laughter)
'Cause there's a but.
In the US today, your zip code predicts your life expectancy,
your race, your wealth.
And your parents’ income predicts your future.
That ain't democratic.
And it's getting worse.
The top one percent of Americans control as much wealth
as the entire bottom 90 percent of the country combined.
And according to one source,
CEOs now make 281 times more
than average workers.
281 times more?
What the hell is wrong with us?
Are CEOs 281 times more talented?
Are they 281 times more deserving?
Are they 281 times harder-working than the rest of us?
Look, we can use the word democracy all we like, but let's be clear.
We've really got more of an oligarchy or a kleptocracy.
Or maybe a monarchy where the kings are billionaires
and reality TV stars, or sometimes both.
(Laughter)
Democracy means
that the kids of house cleaners and mechanics
have the same opportunities in life
as the kids of lawyers and tech execs.
Democracy means that if you work hard,
you can feed your family and afford a place to live.
Democracy means
that power and profit
are distributed democratically.
That is democracy 3.0.
(Applause)
So for those who maybe didn't clap --
(Laughter)
This may be the part in the talk
where some of y'all are getting a little bit nervous.
You hear "economic democracy"
and you think it means enforced sameness.
It does not.
Democracy 3.0 doesn't mean everybody gets an equal house
and an equal income and equal outcomes.
Democracy 3.0 simply means
that everyone gets an equal chance
at the American dream.
Are you with me?
(Applause)
OK, so how do we actually get to democracy 3.0?
Well, the first thing is a shift in mindset.
To start seeing political democracy
and economic democracy as mutually intertwined,
which means we need to advance economic justice
not only for basic fairness, right?
But because that’s the way we strengthen democracy.
And on a practical level,
it means that, yeah, to strengthen democracy,
we need to restore and strengthen the Voting Rights Act,
but also we need to raise wages,
and we need to get money out of politics,
and we need to tax wealth more fairly.
(Applause)
And --
(Applause)
And democracy 3.0 means
that just like voters should have equal voice and power,
workers should have equal voice and power,
and democracy at work means unions.
(Applause and cheers)
In fact, the first wisp of democracy 3.0 was at the last turn of the century,
the last time our country got fed up with extreme wealth and extreme poverty.
That's why we created unions, which helped create the middle class.
And then we created a social safety net,
things like Social Security and eventually Medicare.
Taxing wealth to pay for programs
that would prevent extreme poverty and suffering.
We just need to do it again --
plus do more --
things like universal health care for all.
(Applause)
And more democratic ways of owning businesses,
like employee ownership.
And we need to make sure
that new technologies actually improve our lives
instead of undermining them.
(Cheers and applause)
Look.
The threat to end our democracy
also contains within it
an invitation to make it better.
But our vision cannot be
just to go back to the way things were a few elections ago.
We have a moral and practical imperative
to future-proof democracy by helping each other.
By delivering real political voice
and real economic power
to we, the people,
all of us.
Because if we don't,
if democracy doesn't deliver broad-based opportunity,
people will eventually trade it for something they think will.
And history shows us what happens next.
It's not good for any of us.
Democracy contains within it the tools for its own demise,
but also its renewal.
But if we want a better country, a fairer country,
we're going to have to fight for it.
We, the people, demand
that our politics and our economy work way better
for us and everyone around us,
because democracy can be more
than something we do every couple of years in a voting booth,
but something we can eat
and something we can live in
and something we can put in our pockets
every single day.
That is the only way we are going to save ourselves,
our country,
and the ideals we hold so dear.
Democracy 1.0 gives life to a radical idea.
Democracy 2.0 expands liberty to more and more of us.
Democracy 3.0 can make the pursuit of happiness
possible for all.
Thank you.
(Cheers and applause)
